newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-GROBBELAAR ALMOST QUIT AFTER HEYSEL TRAGEDY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-GROBBELAAR ALMOST QUIT AFTER HEYSEL TRAGEDY.

text.p: Former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar might have avoided his trial on soccer match-fixing charges had he followed his instincts after the Heysel stadium disaster at the 1985 European Cup final.

The Zimbabwean keeper, who won 13 championships and major cups with Liverpool, told a court on Thursday that he had seriously considered quitting soccer after 39 mainly Juventus Italian fans died in a stampede provoked by mainly Liverpool supporters.

"It left very bad scars on myself. I didn't want that element to be associated with the club I loved," he said, prompting his lawyer Rodney Klevan to ask whether the keeper had considered hanging up his gloves.

"Yes. My family and I went to the United States for a holiday and spoke about it for quite some time. I thought that if the thugs wanted to destroy the club and the game I loved, they would win," he said.
Grobbelaar decided to carry on but four years later was on the pitch for the Hillsborough disaster, in which more than 90 fans were crushed to death at an F.A. Cup semifinal.

"The decision was made that we should help with the counselling to help bereaved families. We were on service practically 24 hours a day," said Grobbelaar, who signed for Southampton in 1994 after 13 years with Liverpool.
"My bond with Liverpool is as strong today as when I first signed," he said.

Grobbelaar is accused along with former Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers, ex-Wimbledon and Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim of rigging games to benefit an Asian betting syndicate.
All four deny the charges. Both keepers admit they were paid by Lim for providing match forecasts.
The case against Grobbelaar is based on secretly taped conversations in which he appeared to admit having rigged games for large rewards.

The tapes were recorded by Grobbelaar's former business partner Chris Vincent, who set up a sting operation in which he asked the keeper to throw matches on behalf of a second -- and mythical -- syndicate.
Grobbelaar said he had falsely admitted to both rigging and trying to rig matches in a bid to find out what Vincent was up to. "Were you telling the truth?" asked Klevan.

"No. I told him that lie to get his confidence and to tell him what he wanted to hear. I wanted to know who he was working with," said Grobbelaar, who lost 60,000 pounds ($100,000) when a safari park venture he and Vincent were running folded in July 1994.
The keeper said he had devised a plan to string Vincent along but by the time the two men started talking he had drunk a great deal and became confused.

"I was saying whatever came into my mind. I had a plan, but it went out with the drinking," he said. The Sun newspaper broke the story in November 1994 after its reporters approached Grobbelaar and accused him of rigging games.

"As soon as they came to me, I knew exactly what Vincent had been doing and unfortunately for me, my plan did not work. His did," said the keeper, who faces further questioning about alleged match-rigging on Friday.
